result: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is the most common pediatric spine disorder affecting approximately 3% of children worldwide, yet the molecular genetics and pathology underlying this condition remain ill-defined.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C21, and C24 establish the clinical significance and knowledge gap regarding AIS. These are well-established facts supported by citations to clinical literature and represent accurate characterization of the current state of the field.

result: Genome-wide association studies strongly implicate the ADGRG6 gene for susceptibility to scoliosis in humans.
evaluation: Claims C31, C4, and C9 are supported by citations to published GWAS studies (Kou et al., 2013; Kou et al., 2018). This establishes the genetic rationale for studying ADGRG6 in the context of AIS.

result: ADGRG6 is expressed in multiple spinal tissues including the vertebral growth plate, nucleus pulposus, cartilaginous endplate, annulus fibrosus, and supraspinous ligaments, with distinct Cre driver lines showing tissue-specific recombination patterns.
evaluation: Claims C39-C59 are supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization, immunohistochemistry, and β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures. The expression patterns and Cre recombination profiles are clearly documented with appropriate controls and multiple time points.

result: ADGRG6 expression is significantly reduced in endplate, growth plate, and annulus fibrosus in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant mice at P20.
evaluation: Claims C60 and C61 are supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F with statistical analysis. The reduction is significant in endplate and growth plate, and shows a trend in annulus fibrosus (p=0.068), with stronger significance in scoliotic individuals (p=0.0383).

result: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice display postnatal-onset scoliosis beginning at P20, with approximately 60% penetrance at P20, P40, and P120, Cobb angles ranging from 11° to 46°, and curves centered at thoracic vertebrae T8-T9.
evaluation: Claims C62-C72 are supported by longitudinal X-ray analysis and Cobb angle measurements shown in Figure 2. The data includes appropriate sample sizes (n=23 at P20, n=23 at P40, n=17 at P120), statistical analysis, and controls. The lack of sex bias is supported by Fisher exact test (p=0.2213).

result: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibit wedging of IVDs at the apex of curvature with shifted nucleus pulposus toward the convex side, altered cell distribution, and changes in annulus fibrosus lamellae orientation, without gross patterning defects.
evaluation: Claims C73-C86 are supported by histological data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures. The observations of IVD wedging, nucleus pulposus shift, and altered cell distribution are well-documented with appropriate controls. The inference that local force imbalance drives alterations (C86) is reasonable based on the observation that only IVDs near the curve show changes.

result: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice show reduced SOX9 expression throughout the IVD at P20 in both scoliotic and non-scoliotic mutants, but not at P10, suggesting loss of SOX9 expression is associated with scoliosis initiation.
evaluation: Claims C87-C93 are supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures with quantification (Figure 3G). The temporal relationship between SOX9 reduction and scoliosis onset is well-documented. The inference (C93) is reasonable based on the timing data.

result: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice show altered distribution of COLI-positive cells in the IVD with reduction at the convex side and increase at the concave side, while COLII expression remains normal.
evaluation: Claims C94-C102 are supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3E-M. The normal COLII expression and altered COLI distribution are clearly documented with appropriate controls and multiple tissue regions examined.

result: No significant changes in GAG quantity or specific GAG species were observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mutant IVDs at P20.
evaluation: Claims C103 and C104 are supported by SAX-HPLC data presented in Supplementary file 1. The analysis appropriately identifies chondroitin sulfate and hyaluronan species and shows no significant differences between control and mutant samples.

result: Minor alterations in SOX9 expression may be sufficient to initiate biomechanical instability leading to disc wedging without grossly affecting major ECM components.
evaluation: Claim C105 is a reasonable inference based on the observation that SOX9 is reduced while COLII and GAG proteoglycans are not significantly altered at scoliosis onset. This suggests subtle molecular changes can have significant biomechanical consequences.

result: ADGRG6 regulates pCREB expression in cartilaginous tissues of the spine, with reduced pCREB observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice at P20 and P10.
evaluation: Claims C106-C112 are supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The reduction in pCREB is quantified and statistically significant across multiple tissue types. The temporal relationship (reduction at P10 before scoliosis onset) supports the inference that CREB signaling alterations precede scoliosis.

result: Adgrg6 KO ATDC5 cells show reduced pCREB, and forskolin treatment can stimulate pCREB expression in both WT and KO cells, albeit at reduced levels in KO cells.
evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D-E with n=5 biological replicates and appropriate statistical analysis. The data demonstrate that cAMP signaling can partially bypass ADGRG6 function.

result: Forskolin treatment restores Col10a1 expression and partially restores Sox9 expression in Adgrg6 KO ATDC5 cells, but does not restore Acan or Col2a1 expression, supporting a model where Adgrg6 regulates a subset of genes through cAMP/CREB signaling.
evaluation: Claims C118-C124 are supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The selective rescue of some genes but not others demonstrates specificity in the signaling pathway. The inference (C124) is well-supported by the experimental data.

result: Adgrg6 has no apparent role in mature osteoblasts, as Bglap-Cre; Adgrg6f/f and Sp7Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice show normal spine alignment and bone architecture despite significant reduction in Adgrg6 expression.
evaluation: Claims C125-C133 are supported by X-ray, microCT, histological, and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures. The lack of phenotype despite ~71% reduction in Adgrg6 expression (C131) strongly supports the conclusion that bone quality is not driving scoliosis in the Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f model.

result: Embryonic deletion of Adgrg6 in cartilaginous tissues (ATC; Adgrg6f/f) results in mild susceptibility to scoliosis (25% at P20, 16.7% at P180), while perinatal deletion shows minimal penetrance, suggesting pathogenesis involves tissue-level defects accumulating during embryonic development.
evaluation: Claims C134-C141 are supported by X-ray and Cobb angle data shown in Figure 6A-J with appropriate sample sizes. The comparison between embryonic and perinatal induction strategies provides strong evidence for the developmental timing hypothesis. The lower penetrance compared to Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice (C140) is well-documented.

result: Col2a1-CreERT2-mediated deletion of Adgrg6 shows minimal scoliosis penetrance with perinatal or postnatal induction, confirming that Adgrg6 plays only a minor role in postnatal cartilage regulation for spine alignment.
evaluation: Claims C142-C150 are supported by β-galactosidase staining and X-ray data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2. The low penetrance with postnatal deletion (0% at P30, 14.3% at P90 with P1-P5 induction; 0% with P14-P18 induction) strongly supports the conclusion that embryonic development is critical.

result: Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibit late-onset scoliosis (55.6% at P120, 0% at P40) with curves ranging from 12° to 30°, demonstrating that dense connective tissues are essential for maintaining spine alignment during adult development.
evaluation: Claims C151-C159 are supported by X-ray and histological data shown in Figure 7A-F and supplementary figures. The late onset (after P40) distinguishes this phenotype from the Col2a1-Cre model and supports the conclusion about the role of connective tissues. The speculation about synergy with IVD (C159) is reasonable but requires further testing.

result: Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice exhibit increased tendon cross-sectional area, reduced elastic moduli, and a trend toward reduced failure stress, indicating compromised biomechanical properties of dense connective tissues.
evaluation: Claims C160-C164 are supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 7G-N with appropriate statistical analysis (n=8-9 fascicles from 3 mice). The significant reduction in elastic modulus (p=0.0395) and trend in failure stress (p=0.0589) support the conclusion about compromised biomechanical properties. The inference (C164) linking this to scoliosis pathogenesis is reasonable.

result: ADGRG6 is required in the axial skeleton, intervertebral discs, and dense connective tissues to maintain typical spine alignment through regulation of homeostatic signaling and biomechanical properties.
evaluation: Claims C3, C5, and C165 represent the main conclusion of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental data from multiple conditional knockout models (Col2a1-Cre, ATC, Scx-Cre, Bglap-Cre), expression analysis, histology, and mechanical testing. The tissue-specific requirements are well-established.

result: ADGRG6 regulates biomechanical properties of tendon and stimulates CREB signaling in cartilaginous tissues, with alterations in Adgrg6 signaling through cAMP/CREB being key drivers of scoliosis.
evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C168 are supported by mechanical testing data (Figure 7), pCREB analysis (Figure 4), and forskolin rescue experiments (Figure 4). The integration of these findings provides strong evidence for the signaling mechanism.

result: The findings open up novel therapeutic opportunities for human scoliosis through stimulation of cAMP/CREB signaling.
evaluation: Claims C10, C169, and C214 are speculative statements about potential therapeutic applications. While the forskolin experiments in cell culture (C8) provide proof-of-concept, no in vivo therapeutic studies are presented. Translation to human therapy would require extensive additional validation including efficacy, safety, and delivery studies in animal models before clinical application.

result: Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice represent a unique genetic model of AIS with construct validity, reflecting the natural history of AIS and derived from disruption of a gene associated with AIS in humans.
evaluation: Claims C166 and C167 are supported by the comprehensive phenotypic characterization showing postnatal onset, progressive curvature, and pathological features similar to human AIS, combined with the genetic basis from GWAS studies. The model demonstrates good construct validity as defined by Willner (1984).

result: The pathology observed in Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice recapitulates key features of human AIS including IVD wedging, shifted nucleus pulposus, and IVD degeneration.
evaluation: Claims C170-C178 are supported by citations to clinical studies and the histological data from the mouse model. The parallel between human AIS pathology and the mouse model phenotype strengthens the translational relevance of the findings.

result: Adgrg6 is vital for cartilaginous endplate physiology, and cartilage-specific ablation during embryonic development increases scoliosis susceptibility, supporting a model where cartilaginous tissue regulation plays a crucial role in scoliosis initiation.
evaluation: Claims C179-C182 are supported by the endplate defect observations (C179, citing Liu et al., 2019) and the ATC; Adgrg6f/f data showing increased penetrance with embryonic deletion. The inference about the crucial role of cartilaginous tissues (C182) is well-supported by the experimental evidence.

result: cAMP signaling has chondroprotective effects, positively regulates SOX9, and forskolin can activate pCREB and partially restore Sox9 expression in the absence of Adgrg6 function.
evaluation: Claims C183-C191 integrate prior knowledge (supported by citations) with the current experimental data from ATDC5 cell culture experiments. The mechanistic understanding of the cAMP/CREB/SOX9 pathway is well-established in the literature and confirmed by the forskolin rescue experiments.

result: Embryonic deletion of Adgrg6 leads to subtle structural or biomechanical changes that increase susceptibility to scoliosis during rapid skeletal growth, despite Adgrg6 being largely dispensable for spine patterning and IVD formation.
evaluation: Claims C192-C194 are supported by the temporal analysis showing normal development at P10 but scoliosis onset at P20, combined with the increased penetrance with embryonic versus postnatal deletion. The inference about subtle changes increasing susceptibility during growth periods is reasonable and consistent with the data.

result: The heritability of scoliosis is not explained solely by ADGRG6 variants, and other loci including CREB5 and SOX9 are implicated by GWAS analysis.
evaluation: Claims C195 and C196 are supported by citations to GWAS studies showing that ADGRG6 variants explain only 1-2% of heritability and that other genes in the pathway are also associated with AIS. This provides context for the polygenic nature of the disease.

result: ADGRG6 has no apparent functional role in bone-forming osteoblasts, contrasting with a recent report by Sun et al. (2020), with discrepancies potentially explained by off-target effects of the Sp7-Cre transgene.
evaluation: Claims C197-C204 are supported by the experimental data from Bglap-Cre and Sp7-Cre models showing no phenotype, contrasted with the Sun et al. report. The discussion of potential Cre artifacts (C204) is supported by citations to prior research on this issue and represents a reasonable explanation for the discrepancy.

result: Scx-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice show high penetrance scoliosis comparable to Col2a1-Cre; Adgrg6f/f mice, with reduced elastic moduli in tendons, suggesting scoliosis is primarily driven by biomechanical instability of paraspinal tendons and ligaments.
evaluation: Claims C205-C212 are supported by the X-ray data showing comparable penetrance (55.6% vs ~60%), mechanical testing data showing reduced elastic modulus, and citations to clinical studies linking connective tissue disorders to scoliosis. The inference about biomechanical instability (C212) is well-supported by the mechanical testing results.

result: Biomechanical defects in cartilaginous and dense connective tissues due to defective ADGRG6/cAMP/CREB signaling underlie the pathogenesis of AIS.
evaluation: Claim C213 represents the central mechanistic conclusion of the study, integrating findings from multiple conditional knockout models, signaling studies, and mechanical testing. This is well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript.
